item.title: Nagasaki Turkey Rice — Guide
item.description: Turkey rice (toruko rice) is one of Nagasaki’s most beloved and quirkily named local dishes — and, despite the name, it contains no turkey at all. Instead it’s a generous, all-in-one plate that brings together three things at once: a portion of pilaf or fried rice, a nest of spaghetti in meat or tomato sauce, and a crispy breaded pork cutlet (tonkatsu), usually finished with a drizzle of demi-glace or curry sauce.

item.title: Toyama Black Ramen: A Salty, Soy-Dark Local Noodle Classic — Guide
item.description: Toyama Black Ramen is defined by its distinctively dark, intensely salty soy-based broth, a local noodle dish originally created in the postwar years as a hearty, high-sodium meal meant to replace salt lost by factory workers through sweat during physically demanding shifts. The broth’s dark colour comes from a generous amount of dark soy sauce, and the dish is typically topped with black pepper, chashu pork, bamboo shoots and scallions, remaining a defining local comfort food found in ramen shops throughout Toyama City today.

item.title: Omurice at Urawa Retro Cafes: A Nostalgic Comfort Food Trail — Guide
item.description: Urawa’s cluster of old-fashioned kissaten (retro cafes) has made the neighbourhood a low-key pilgrimage site for fans of omurice — a soft, gently cooked omelette wrapped over ketchup-seasoned fried rice, a beloved Japanese comfort food dish with Western-influenced origins. These cafes, many decorated in a warm, unchanged 1970s-80s aesthetic of wood panelling and vintage furniture, serve the dish alongside strong drip coffee, offering an unhurried, nostalgic dining experience distinct from Tokyo’s trendier cafe scene.

item.title: Obanzai Guide: Kyoto's Home-Style Comfort Cooking
item.description: If kaiseki is Kyoto’s formal art, obanzai is its soul food: the everyday home cooking of Kyoto households, built on local seasonal vegetables, simple techniques, frugality, and quiet good taste. Obanzai is what Kyoto people actually eat at home — small dishes of simmered vegetables, tofu, beans, dried fish, and pickles, made to use ingredients fully and waste nothing. For visitors tired of heavy or touristy food, an obanzai meal is a revelation: gentle, healthy, deeply satisfying, and authentically Kyoto.

item.title: Taco Rice Guide: Okinawa's Tex-Mex Soul Food & Where to Eat
item.description: Taco rice is Okinawa’s quintessential fusion comfort food — seasoned taco-style ground beef, shredded lettuce, tomato and cheese piled over a bowl of white rice. Born near the American military bases in the 1980s as a cheap, filling meal for hungry servicemen, it crossed over into local life and is now an Okinawan icon. Hearty, cheap and crowd-pleasing, it’s a delicious window into the island’s deep American cultural layer. This guide covers its origins, what’s in it, where to eat it and how to order.
